where: Pricing file, the lock after an unpaid trial
q: When someone ends the free month without paying, their account is locked to reading. How long do we keep that account?
a: Keep it with no end date: nothing is ever deleted, as the app promises.
b: Close it after a year with no sign-in, after a warning email.
rec: A, because the app already tells people nothing is deleted, and the law does not ask us to erase it.

where: Pricing file, the lock after an unpaid trial
q: While an account is locked after an unpaid free month, should changes the person makes in their own GitHub or Google Drive copy still flow back into frontmatter?
a: No. Syncing pauses both ways and catches up in one go when they pay; their GitHub or Drive copy is never touched.
b: Yes. Keep pulling their changes in, so what they read in frontmatter stays current.
rec: A, because pulling changes in means writing to a locked account, which is editing by another name.

where: Pricing file, the lock after an unpaid trial
q: Every new account starts with a free month of Pro. If someone does not pay at the end, can they carry on with the free plan, or must they pay to edit at all?
a: They can choose the free plan. Editing comes back within the free limits, and nothing above those limits is lost.
b: Paying is the only way to edit again. The free plan is then never reachable by anyone who signs up after launch.
rec: A, because B quietly removes the free plan that the pricing page and the free AI setup are built for.

where: Pricing file and support file, the lock after an unpaid trial
q: You chose to block downloads when a free month ends unpaid. Indian and European privacy law give people a right to take their data with them. Is blocking the download legal?
a: Ship the block as decided, and get a lawyer's written opinion before the first stranger signs up.
b: Leave downloads open during the lock until a lawyer says the block is legal, and lock only editing and copying.
rec: B, because turning the block on later is cheap, and a complaint to a regulator is not.

where: Support and lifecycle file, what happens if frontmatter shuts down
q: If frontmatter ever shuts down, should people whose free month ended unpaid be allowed to download their documents before the end?
a: Yes. At shutdown the lock lifts for downloads, so nobody leaves without their files.
b: No. The lock stays, and only paying and never-locked accounts can download.
rec: A, because we promise that downloads are the last thing we switch off, and B makes that untrue for some people.

q: The app used to promise "every document stays readable and downloadable". Your trial decision made that untrue, so the promise is reworded. Do you approve the new wording: "Your documents always stay readable, and nothing is deleted. Editing, copying and export stay open on every plan, and pause only if a trial ends unpaid."?
a: Approve it as written.
b: Rewrite it, for example to name the free plan once the answer to N3 is known.
rec: A, because it is true in every state today; revisit only if N3 or N4 changes the lock.

where: Decision record on moving accounts to the company, the domain row
q: The frontmatter.in web address is registered at GoDaddy until June 2029, but the public record hides whose account it sits in. Whose account holds it, and will you move it to the company as you decided for every other account?
a: Check the GoDaddy account now and move the address to the company's account before the first stranger signs up.
b: Leave it where it is until the company's other accounts are moved, then move them together.
rec: A, because losing the web address is the one account failure that takes the whole product offline, and the check takes minutes.

q: Windows shows a scary "unknown publisher" warning unless the app is signed with a certificate the company buys. Microsoft's own signing service is closed to Indian companies. Which certificate should the company buy?
a: A: Certum Standard, from €139 on the list price, in the company's name
b: B: Certum EV, from €329, or Sectigo, from $536.25 a year on a five-year term
rec: A: Microsoft now says the dearer EV kind no longer removes the warning faster, so the extra money buys nothing we need

q: Building everything you have asked for takes about 245 to 352 weeks (4.7 to 6.8 years) at today's pace of roughly one working day a week, and the paid launch comes about 209 to 276 weeks in. Do we accept that, or shorten it?
a: Accept the full plan at today's pace, with nothing moved.
b: Shorten it. One extra working day a week cuts the total to 141 to 178 weeks, two days to 102 to 123, three to 82 to 96; separately, moving voice typing and PDF conversion to after launch brings launch 33 to 43 weeks sooner.
rec: B, two extra days a week plus voice and PDF after launch: launch in about 73 to 82 weeks, because deferring alone still leaves launch 3.4 to 4.5 years away.

q: If the trial with twenty outside people misses its minimum (for example, fewer than four still using it in week two), do we keep building everything anyway?
a: Pause the build for one meeting of both founders, then choose to continue, change the order or stop.
b: Keep building regardless, and use the trial only to adjust.
rec: A, because building on regardless turns the trial into a formality, while an automatic stop would contradict your answer to build everything.

q: Do you approve the proposed way sheets, boards and mixed files are saved: a sheet as an ordinary table in a document with its formulas written just below it, a board as a folder with one small file per card, and one embedded file shown by a link to the original, never a copy?
a: Approve all three as the basis for building.
b: Hold them until a small prototype of each has been tried.
rec: A, because every file people write will carry these formats, each record lists what would reverse it, and the first build step is itself the prototype.

q: When someone turns a finished project plan into a task board, should that use up one of their plan credits?
a: No extra credit: it counts as part of the plan they already paid for.
b: It uses one credit, like making a new plan.
rec: A, because it is one small extra AI call on a plan the person already paid for.

q: When you move your own card on a board, or rename your own column, should it save at once, or wait for you to approve it like every change from someone else?
a: It saves at once, like your own typing; only changes from other people, AI and agents wait for approval.
b: It waits in the list of changes to approve, like everything else.
rec: A, because approving your own drag turns one action into two, and your own typing already saves at once.

q: Our one-line description says "a markdown editor". Now that the product also does sheets and boards, should the line change?
a: Keep "a markdown editor".
b: Widen it to name documents, sheets and boards.
rec: A, because every new kind is still a plain text file reviewed the same way, and listing kinds reads like the all-in-one suites we stand against.

q: Are these starting limits right: free users get 60 minutes of voice typing a month and PDFs up to 1,000 pages and 100 MB; paid users get 300 minutes and 200 scanned PDF pages read by AI a month?
a: Start with these, and change them from the settings panel once real costs are measured.
b: Start lower until costs are measured.
rec: A, because the limits can be changed without a release, which is how the free document limit is already handled. If the voice and PDF log asks the same, answer once.

q: About thirty working days of writing (templates, help text, question sets, empty screens) is not assigned to anyone. Who writes it?
a: The two founders, each piece in the same step as the feature it explains.
b: Hire or commission a writer.
rec: A, because the text has to match features as they land, and no budget for a writer exists yet.

q: How many minutes of voice typing should each plan get a month, topped up a little each day rather than all at once on the 1st?
a: Free 60 minutes, Pro 300 minutes
b: Free 60 minutes, Pro 600 minutes
rec: A, because 600 could eat up to 85 per cent of what a Pro subscription earns us if fully used, and 60 already beats Wispr's free plan.

q: When someone dictates, how much should the app tidy their words by default? They can change it in settings.
a: Medium: remove ums and false starts, add punctuation, split paragraphs, turn spoken lists into lists, keep their own words
b: Low: only remove ums and add punctuation, change nothing else
rec: A, because it gives tidy paragraphs and lists while every word stays the speaker's own.

q: When the app tidies what someone said, should the tidied text wait for one key press (Tab) before it counts, or go straight into the document the way Wispr Flow does?
a: Wait for one key press; the raw words appear instantly while the tidy-up runs
b: Go straight in, with no key press
rec: A, because it keeps our promise that no AI change lands unseen, and the person never waits for it.

q: Before voice typing launches, switch off Groq's setting that keeps voice recordings for up to 30 days for abuse checks, and note the date you did it.
a: Switch it off before launch
b: Leave Groq's default on
rec: A, because we promise that voice recordings are not kept anywhere.

q: Sign in to Groq, read the free account's real daily limits for speech, then send one 3-second test clip to see whether it uses 10 seconds of the free daily allowance.
a: Do it before the voice test runs
b: Skip it, and plan on the smaller reading
rec: A, because the free allowance is shared by every user and the plan's arithmetic depends on it.

q: How big a PDF may someone convert at once? The conversion runs on their own computer or phone.
a: The same on Free and Pro: up to 1,000 pages, 100 MB, and 100 scanned pages
b: Smaller limits on Free, to give people a reason to upgrade
rec: A, because conversion costs us nothing and the limits only protect the person's own browser tab.

q: Pro can have an AI read scanned pages more accurately than the free reader, up to 200 pages a month. Should it be switched on the day the PDF converter launches?
a: Off at launch; on once our test pages show it reads accurately
b: On at launch
rec: A, because no AI reader has been tried on our test pages yet, and the free reader is already there as the fallback.

q: When someone fills a new, empty document from a PDF and presses Accept on the preview, should that Accept count as their approval, or should the text also wait in the list of changes to approve?
a: The Accept counts; the history still records that a converter wrote it
b: It also waits in the list of changes
rec: A, because they have just read and accepted that exact text, and nothing of theirs is overwritten.

q: Ask the lawyer already reviewing the paid-trial lock whether India's data protection law needs a separate consent for voice recordings.
a: Add it to the opinion already being sought
b: Launch voice without asking
rec: A, because it adds one question to advice already being paid for, and the app asks once meanwhile.

q: A strong PDF tool, Marker, has a licence that bars products competing with its maker's. Should we pay a lawyer to check whether we could use it anyway?
a: No; the converter does not need it
b: Yes; get an opinion
rec: A, because the free tools we chose already do the job, and the opinion would cost money for an option we are not taking.
